chapter_theme: Neelakesi, debating the Buddha in his own city, attacks his account of karma and his first truth: she argues that the rule making killing and theft depend on knowledge and intention would excuse a man who kills, robs or abducts by mistake, while intent without a deed still binds; then she argues that 'all is suffering', 'all is impure' and 'nothing stays' each undo the four noble truths and every reason for conduct.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in his own city in the புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்; addressed as வாமன் and நாதன்

538.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddha will not speak of things that have no fruit, then what his followers say about persons (புற்கலர்) dying could count as truth only if something were held to persist, and nothing in his teaching matches that.
538.nuance: Line 1 (களபாவமாம்) and line 4 (ஏவனன்றென்றி) resist division; the reading rests on புற்கலர் (pudgala, the 'person') and சாவ (dying) in lines 2 and 3, and on the frame of the argument against a doctrine with no lasting self.

539.reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's teaching that killing, lust and theft are deeds of the body and asks how that can be, when without a mind no one is there in any place to do such deeds.
539.nuance: The Buddhist grouping is by the door a deed goes out through (body, speech, mind, as 526 set out); Neelakesi reads it as if the body were said to act alone. The same three bodily deeds open the Manimekalai teacher's list of ten evil deeds.

claims.claim: killing, lust and theft are the deeds that arise in the body
no deed of the body is done without a mind that does it

540.reading: Neelakesi lists deeds that harm without a chosen victim (planting thorns on a path, burning a house, pushing people into a pit, despoiling temple vessels, driving an elephant at people) and asks whether these do not bring blame and sin.
540.nuance: The list prepares the attack on the five conditions of killing in 541: in none of these deeds does the doer know and intend a particular life. கோயிற் கலஞ்செய்தல் may mean damaging the temple's vessels or something else done to them; the sense of harm is clear from the frame.

claims.claim: deeds that harm whoever happens to meet them bring blame and sin though no particular victim was intended

541.reading: Neelakesi restates the Buddha's rule that a killing is a killing only when five things meet: a life joined to a body, the thought 'this is a life', the intention 'I will destroy it', the deed done with that fault, and the death.
541.nuance: The rule is stated here in order to be answered: 543 to 550 bring cases of mistaken identity in which, by this rule, a man would die or be robbed with no sin incurred. ஐந்தில் (line 4) names the five; their list is read from lines 1 to 4.

claims.claim: a killing counts as killing only when there is a living being, knowledge that it lives, the intention to kill, the act, and death

542.reading: Neelakesi tests the intention rule from the side of worship: if a man, thinking 'this is the god', bows in devotion but has in fact bowed to something other than the god, does he incur fault or not?
542.nuance: The verse is a question whose answer is left for the hearer; தாவனை in line 4 (what was wrongly worshipped) and தூவென மும்மையே தோற்றி in line 3 are hard to fix, so the exact case is uncertain.

claims.claim: whether an act brings merit or fault depends on what the mind took its object to be

543.reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Buddhists say a man who stabs someone resembling his enemy, taking him for that enemy, incurs no killing-karma, and bids them consider how the person stabbed nonetheless died.
543.nuance: The answer is the plain fact of line 4 (செத்தவாறு): a man is dead, and the rule of intention cannot make him alive. The verse sets the pattern of resemblance (ஒத்தவன்) that 549 repeats for theft (ஒப்பது).

claims.claim: one who kills a man mistaking him for his enemy incurs no karma of killing
a death that one's deed causes is a killing whatever the doer took the victim to be

544.reading: Neelakesi says that, by the Buddhists' own words, even when someone dies no sin of killing follows, because the doer's mind did not go out and reach that victim.
544.nuance: Line 1 to 2 (குறட்கண்ணும் ஒன்றுமே ... எப்பாரியார) are obscure; the verse repeats 313 of the Mokkala debate word for word, so the editor or the tradition placed the same argument in both debates.

claims.claim: the sin of killing follows only when the killer's mind reached the one who died

545.reading: Neelakesi argues that where the intended enemy did not die, the Buddhist must either deny the sin of the hostile intention or charge it to the other life that was killed, and she bids him hear how karma truly works, citing one who worshipped a wicked man and was ruined.
545.nuance: பட்டிலன் (line 1, 'he did not die') fixes the case as a failed or misdirected killing; line 3 (துட்டனைத் தொழுதோன் துறந்தான்) alludes to a story the verse does not tell, and the reading of lines 2 and 3 is a guess.

claims.claim: a hostile intention binds karma even when the deed falls on someone other than its target

546.reading: Neelakesi argues that if karma binds only when all five conditions are met, then in a case the Buddhists themselves tell, where no one died, it would be unfitting that the doer went to the fierce Avici hell for splitting Kalakan.
546.nuance: The verse turns on a story it only names (அவீசி, the hell; காந்தி, பாலி and கலகன், unidentified here); that the case is a Buddhist one in which no death occurs is read from வீய்ந்ததின்மையின் (line 2) and the argument.

claims.claim: karma binds only when all five conditions of the deed are met

547.reading: Neelakesi says that the man who sets out to kill though his sharp weapon fails, the man who sets out for another's house, and the burglar all carry the dark deed of their intent, and the world and kin are bound with the one who speaks it.
547.nuance: Here Neelakesi grants intention its weight; her case against the Buddha is not that the mind does not matter but that mind and deed both bind, so a failed intent and an unintended death each carry karma. Line 4 (சொல்லுவானோடு உலகமுஞ் சுற்றமே) is unclear.

claims.claim: the intention to kill, to go to another's wife or to steal binds evil karma even when the act fails

548.reading: Neelakesi presses the Buddha on a case involving contact with women, saying that his claim not to reckon karma from such contact does not survive even being stated.
548.nuance: Nearly every line is obscure (துப்பினால் in line 1, வப்பினார் முலை காய்வது in line 2); the Buddha is addressed as வாமன் as in 517. The claim is read from the frame of 541 to 550.

claims.claim: contact without intention brings no karma

549.reading: Neelakesi states the Buddhist rule on theft: if a man takes a thing that resembles what he once deposited, believing it his own, there is no fault whether he carries it off or keeps it, for even when seen it is not theft.
549.nuance: The rule is answered by the satire of 550, which applies the same reasoning to another man's wife.

claims.claim: taking another's thing in the belief that it is one's own is not theft

550.reading: Neelakesi mocks the rule: let a man carry off a householder's wife asleep at home, telling himself 'this is she' (his own wife, whose soft feet ached from walking by day), and take her by deceit, crying 'long live the Buddha'.
550.nuance: The verse is a reductio: it adds nothing to the rule of 549 but its consequence. The cry வாழ்க புத்தன் puts the Buddha's name on the abduction.

claims.claim: if mistaken belief excused the deed, a man could carry off another's wife without fault

551.reading: Neelakesi says that, having laid waste the aggregates by showing them to be as unreal as a crow's teeth since nothing binds them into one, she will now shatter with a few words the noble truths he taught and the mind as well.
551.nuance: காகதந்தம் (crow's teeth) is a stock example of a thing that does not exist. ஆரிய சத்தை (line 3) names the noble truths, which 553 to 562 take up.
551.event: Neelakesi turns from the aggregates to attack the Buddha's noble truths.

claims.claim: the five aggregates, with nothing binding them into one, are as unreal as a crow's teeth

552.reading: The verse gives the Buddhist account that the body-heap, though one, is viewed apart as five, and a challenge to show here the truth that was seen; Neelakesi answers that she will speak of suffering and of awareness.
552.nuance: The speaker of lines 1 to 3 may be the Buddha (கொண்டுநின்றாம், கண்டநா மெய்ம்மை, 'we held', 'the truth we saw') and line 4 Neelakesi's reply (கூறுவோம்); the verse has no speech marker but எனின், and ஆகுலம் in line 4 is read as distress.

claims.claim: the one heap of the body is analysed into five aggregates

553.reading: Neelakesi argues that if all is suffering, then good things too become worthless the moment one says so; the teaching is therefore faulty, and since suffering admits no plurality, the fool was wrong to say there are four truths.
553.nuance: The argument needs the Buddhist to hold that the third and fourth truths, cessation and the path, are themselves suffering; the Manimekalai's teacher gives release as joy (இன்பம் வீடே), which the reductio does not meet.

claims.claim: all is suffering
if everything is suffering there can be only one truth, not four

554.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the flawless truth is to see the three kinds of suffering together, then the Buddha, having spoken that truth, erred in saying he gave joy to others.
554.nuance: உழப்பு மூன்றும் (line 1) is read as the three kinds of suffering; line 4 (பழுக்களே காய்வது ...) is corrupt or obscure and is left unread.

claims.claim: seeing the three kinds of suffering together is the noble truth
one who teaches that all is suffering cannot claim to give others joy

555.reading: Neelakesi argues that if all is suffering, every deed is one and its fruit must be equal, so the Buddhists cannot say that others have fallen into low births while their own people rise, or that their path is the highest.

claims.claim: if all is suffering, deeds and their fruits are all alike and no path is higher than another

556.reading: Neelakesi tells the Buddha that if the end of everything is only suffering with no joy, he should stop giving counsel and guarding conduct, go a little into fire, and not seek shade, since every act only adds to endless suffering.
556.nuance: The verse drives 'all is suffering' to its practical end: if there is no joy anywhere, fire and shade are alike, and so are virtue and vice.

claims.claim: a teaching that all is suffering with no joy leaves no reason to teach or keep conduct

557.reading: Neelakesi argues that if his word that nothing at all is pure is true, then all who wear garlands and sandal paste have failed to find the safe good path.
557.nuance: The verse does not say whose garlands are meant; it may point at the Buddhists' own worship with garland and sandal, or at all householders, so the force of the consequence is uncertain. Naladiyar 48, a Jain quatrain, says just this of those who praise sandal and garland.

claims.claim: nothing at all is pure

558.reading: Neelakesi points out that the Buddhist says his recitation, conduct and food are flawless and pure, and asks what, then, he calls impure; the Lord, she says, knew other things very well.
558.nuance: நாதன் நீ பிற நன்கறிந்தாய் (line 4) is irony.

claims.claim: the monks' recitation, conduct and food are pure
one who calls all things impure cannot call his own practice pure

559.reading: Neelakesi, whose shoulders surpass the bamboo, says that the bowl-carrying monkeys who ignore the truth the Buddha spoke burn with anger, saying 'we are pure and others are impure'.
559.nuance: கவி மண்டைகள் (line 3) joins monkey and begging bowl as an insult to the monks; the narrator's line names Neelakesi as the speaker by her shoulders.

claims.claim: monks who call themselves pure and others impure have ignored their own teacher's truth

560.reading: Neelakesi argues that if even those who saw the right path long ago gain no purity afterward, then for one who takes whatever arises day by day as its nature, there is nothing that could have made things impure.
560.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (இன்றுமின்று மியல்வது வாக்கொள்வாய்க்கு இன்றித் தூய்தன்மை) are hard to divide; the reading joins the momentariness of 562 to the purity argument of 557 to 561.

claims.claim: whatever arises moment by moment is simply its own nature

561.reading: Neelakesi tells the fools who said all is impure to smear themselves with rot, bathe in the gutter, and gulp the filth that vultures and pigs eat, since by their teaching none of it differs from anything else.
561.nuance: தூய்தன்மை in line 4 is தூய்து அன்மை, 'not being pure'. Line 3 (மெழுகுமின்னிடை மெச்சியமல்லதின்) is obscure.

claims.claim: if all things are impure there is no ground to choose clean over foul

562.reading: Neelakesi argues that if he says things do not stay, the saying itself does not stay, and if he says 'we are not', his own happy thesis is spoiled; since all is the same as itself, she asks, good one, how will he establish the four truths he spoke.
562.nuance: The verse is in a longer metre than its neighbours. நல்லாய் (line 4) addresses the opponent as 'good one', ironically. Line 3 (எல்லாந் தானே யென்றலினேன் விழவெய்தி) is not secure.

claims.claim: nothing endures beyond the moment
a doctrine of momentariness cannot establish any thesis, including the four truths

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists killing, theft and lust as the three evil deeds that arise in the body; 539 takes that very grouping and asks who does them if the mind is not there.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic sorts deeds by the door they go out through and counts the mind's three faults separately, so the Jain objection works only by reading a classification of doors as a claim that the body acts without mind.

links.note: In 259 the monk says nothing exists but the mind and evil conduct is not evil karma; 541 states the Buddhist rule that a killing needs knowledge and intention as well as a death.
links.teaches: The earlier boast that only the mind counts becomes a precise five-part rule here, and the precision is what lets Neelakesi build cases of mistaken identity in which a man dies and no killing is counted.

links.note: Kural 282 says even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; 547 holds that the burglar, the would-be killer and the would-be adulterer carry the karma of their intent even when the act fails.
links.teaches: Read beside a debate that also condemns the unintended killing, the couplet's thought-crime proves to be only half of the Jain position, which binds karma both to the intent without the deed and to the deed without the intent.

gains.a: the verse's claim that a failed intent binds finds a rule in the Kural that gives the same verdict on theft without any doctrine of karma
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'thinking is wrong' is set inside an account of why: the intent itself binds karma, and a deed done in error binds it too

links.note: 553 argues that if all is suffering there cannot be four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives four truths in which the fourth is joy, which is release caused by not clinging.
links.teaches: The reductio holds only against a Buddhism that calls everything suffering without exception; the Buddhist epic's own fourth truth (இன்பம் வீடே) is the exception, which shows the Jain argument aimed at a version the Buddhist teacher would not accept.

links.note: 256 mocks 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; 556 draws its practical consequence, that with no joy anywhere one may as well walk into fire.
links.teaches: The poet attacks the first truth twice in two tones, as a lazy monk's grumble in the Arkkachandra debate and as an argument against the Buddha himself that the doctrine would remove every reason for conduct.

links.note: Naladiyar 48 says those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen what the body is; 557 treats 'those who wear garlands and sandal have not found the path' as the absurd outcome of the Buddhist claim that nothing is pure.
links.teaches: A Jain anthology and a Jain epic part ways on impurity: the Naladiyar finds it in the body and condemns the garland, while the Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist 'nothing at all is pure' because extended to everything it erases the difference between path and no path.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to aim at the word 'all', since its own tradition accepts the body's foulness in the same image of sandal and garland
gains.b: the quatrain's contempt for adornment is marked as a claim about the body, which the Jain debater would not let grow into a claim that everything is impure

links.note: 252 says the monks call all things impure yet bow at their own defiled master's feet; 558 says they call their own recitation, conduct and food pure.
links.teaches: The charge of inconsistency grows from the monks' worship of their teacher to their whole daily practice, so the 'all is impure' doctrine is shown to exempt everything its holders do.

links.note: Sivavakkiyar mocks those who bathe daily crying 'pollution', since the body itself took form from pollution; 561 tells those who hold all things impure to bathe in the gutter, as if that conclusion were absurd.
links.teaches: The Siddhar draws the very conclusion the Jain debater uses as a reductio: if everything is born of impurity, the ritual bath is pointless, so the same premise ends in mockery of ritual in one text and in mockery of the premise in the other.

gains.a: the epic's reductio meets a poet who accepts its consequence, showing that the argument holds only for one who still values the clean over the foul
gains.b: the Siddhar's attack on bathing is seen to rest on a premise a Jain epic thought no sane teacher could hold

links.note: 196 asks how perishing can be known if the mind perishes wholly with its objects; 562 asks how a teacher who says nothing stays can establish any thesis, the four truths included.
links.teaches: Neelakesi uses one argument against momentariness in both debates, first against the knowing of perishing and here against the stating of doctrine, so the self-refutation of the momentary becomes the Neelakesi's standing reply to Buddhism.

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word: வாழ்க புத்தன் (550 line 4), புத்தனீர் (543 line 3), புத்தரே (544 line 3)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word: கந்தமாவன (551 line 1); 552 counts them as five (ஐந்து)

source_issues: Verse 544 repeats verse 313 (Mokkala debate) word for word.
Verse 538: lines 1 and 4 (களபாவமாம், ஏவனன்றென்றி) are hard to divide and may be corrupt.
Verse 548, lines 1-2 (துப்பினால், வப்பினார்முலை காய்வது வாமனீ) are obscure; the line division may be faulty.
Verse 554, line 4 (பழுக்களே காய்வது ண்டுமுண் டேபிற) has a stray ண்டு and looks corrupt.
Verse 562 is in a longer metre than the verses around it, and its line 3 (யென்றலி னேன் விழவெய்தி) looks corrupt.
Verse 543, line 2: யில்லைனப் probably for இல்லையெனப்.
